They cause hypertension, diabetes, infection risk and osteoporosis, especially problematic where monitoring is limited.
Start anti‑TB therapy and delay immunosuppression until infection is controlled.
faq.q: What is the first step if a patient with suspected lupus tests positive for TB?

exam: What bedside findings would point toward systemic lupus rather than infection‑related fever? — Symmetric arthritis, malar rash, oral ulcers, proteinuria; infection lacks these patterns.

A patient with new joint pain and positive ANA lives in a malaria‑endemic area. How do you differentiate autoimmune arthritis from post‑malaria arthralgia? — Look for persistent swelling, morning stiffness >30 min, radiographic erosions; malaria arthralgia resolves within weeks.

You have limited lab capacity and cannot obtain anti‑dsDNA. Which clinical criteria allow you to start treatment for lupus? — Presence of ≥4 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria (e.g., rash, renal involvement, hematologic abnormalities) permits early therapy.

Why is methotrexate preferred over azathioprine for rheumatoid arthritis in a patient with hepatitis B? — Methotrexate has less risk of viral reactivation; azathioprine can exacerbate hepatitis B replication.

A patient on high‑dose steroids develops fever and cough in a TB‑high region. What is your next step? — Rule out active TB before continuing steroids; obtain sputum microscopy/ GeneXpert; start empiric anti‑TB if suspicion high.

Explain how you would monitor for steroid‑induced osteoporosis in a setting without DEXA scans. — Use clinical risk assessment (age, duration >3 months, low calcium diet) and give calcium/vitamin D supplementation; consider plain spine X‑ray if fractures suspected.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate referral for possible lupus nephritis? — New onset edema with proteinuria >0.5 g/day or rising creatinine.

How does schistosomiasis infection complicate the diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis? — It can cause eosinophilia and elevated transaminases, mimicking autoimmune hepatitis; stool microscopy and serology help differentiate.
ai.title: Autoimmune Diseases Overview
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Autoimmune diseases result from immune‑mediated damage to self‑tissues. Diagnosis relies on clinical patterns, auto‑antibodies and exclusion of infections common in low‑resource settings. Management combines immunosuppression, treatment of triggers and prevention of organ damage.

b: Core criteria: compatible clinical picture + at least one specific auto‑antibody (e.g., ANA, anti‑dsDNA, anti‑CCP) + exclusion of infection or drug‑induced mimic.
sections.p: A disorder in which the immune system attacks host organs, producing characteristic clinical syndromes and often detectable auto‑antibodies.

t.b: Identifies organ involvement and triggers; guides targeted antibody testing.
Confirms autoimmune etiology; positive result supports diagnosis, negative does not exclude.

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, ESR/CRP, renal & liver function)
t.b: Detect organ inflammation or damage; guide urgency of treatment.

t.a: Infection screen (HIV, TB, hepatitis B/C, malaria where endemic)
t.b: Rules out infectious mimics that can cause similar serology; treat if positive before immunosuppression.

b: Mild: limited organ involvement, normal function.
Moderate: organ dysfunction but no life‑threatening features.
Severe: organ failure, high inflammatory markers, or rapid progression.
sections.p: Severity is organ‑specific; common tools include SLEDAI for lupus, DAS28 for rheumatoid arthritis, and NYHA class for cardiac involvement.

b: Genetic predisposition (HLA‑DR alleles).
Infections prevalent in East Africa (HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis) that can break tolerance.
Herbal medicines containing immunostimulants.
Occupational exposures (silica, pesticides).
sections.p: Autoimmunity arises from genetic susceptibility, environmental triggers and dysregulated immune regulation.

b: Systemic: fever, fatigue, weight loss.
Joint: symmetric polyarthritis, morning stiffness.
Skin: malar rash, photosensitivity, discoid lesions.
Renal: hematuria, proteinuria, edema.
Neurologic: peripheral neuropathy, seizures (SLE).
sections.p: Presentation varies by disease but often includes constitutional symptoms, organ‑specific pain or dysfunction, and characteristic skin or joint findings.
Targeted testing confirms autoimmunity, assesses organ damage and excludes mimics.

t.b: Detects active urinary sediment; casts or dysmorphic RBCs suggest lupus nephritis.
Looks for pleural effusion or interstitial changes; may be normal in early disease.
Assesses pericardial effusion or valvular disease; absence does not rule out early cardiac involvement.

t.a: If imaging unavailable: focused bedside ultrasound
t.b: Detects effusions or organ enlargement; guides urgent referral.

b: Rapidly rising creatinine or proteinuria → renal failure.
New neurological deficits → CNS vasculitis.
Severe anemia or thrombocytopenia → bone‑marrow suppression.
Cardiac tamponade signs (hypotension, muffled heart sounds).
sections.p: Unchecked autoimmunity can rapidly damage vital organs.

b: First‑line: glucocorticoids (short‑term) to halt acute inflammation.
Steroid‑sparing agents: methotrexate (RA), azathioprine or mycophenolate (SLE, renal disease).
Biologics (e.g., anti‑TNF) when conventional agents fail and are affordable.
Treat underlying infection before immunosuppression (e.g., anti‑TB therapy).
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza before long‑term immunosuppression.
sections.p: Treat the immune trigger, control inflammation and protect affected organs.

b: Clinic review every 3‑6 months with disease activity score.
Baseline and periodic CBC, liver/renal panels.
Screen for osteoporosis if steroids >3 months.
Educate on infection signs; prompt treatment of febrile illness.
sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents irreversible damage and drug toxicity.

b: Infection‑related arthritis (e.g., chikungunya).
Drug‑induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide).
Post‑streptococcal rheumatic fever (joint pain, carditis).
sections.p: Several infectious or drug‑induced conditions mimic autoimmunity.

b: ANA can be positive in chronic infections; interpret with clinical picture.
Low‑titer anti‑CCP may appear in TB; confirm with radiographs.
ESR rises in malaria; not specific for autoimmunity.
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely negative or positive in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision, severe headache, or focal neurological deficit.
Rapidly worsening renal function or anuria.
Signs of cardiac tamponade (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds).
